# Warp and Newton on a machine with no GPU — the run

The question: how much of NVIDIA's simulation stack runs on a computer with
no NVIDIA GPU in it? The two pieces whose documentation says "CPU" — Warp
and Newton — were installed and run here, timed, on 13 September 2026.

## The machine

A cloud Ubuntu 24.04.4 container: 4 vCPUs (Intel Xeon @ 2.10 GHz), 15 GB
RAM, no GPU (`nvidia-smi: command not found`; Warp at start-up: "Could not
find or load the NVIDIA CUDA driver. GPU execution will not be available"),
Python 3.11.15. It is not the M4 Mac the rest of the site is written on;
Newton's README lists macOS as "CPU only", which is the same path.

## The install

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate
time pip install warp-lang "newton[examples]"
```

1 min 20 s wall (0m39.959s user, 0m25.778s sys), a 2.8 GB virtual
environment. What pip chose: `newton 1.6.0`, `warp-lang 1.17.0`, `warp-nn
0.3.1`, `mujoco 3.12.0` and `mujoco-warp 3.12.0` (PyPI had 3.13.0 that day;
Newton 1.6.0 pins the earlier one), `newton-usd-schemas 0.5.0`, `usd-core
26.3`, `pyglet 2.1.16`.

## A Warp kernel

[`saxpy.py`](https://github.com/Collegica/collegica/tree/main/docs/research/2026-09-13-nvidia-robotics/notes/saxpy.py): a 10-million-element `y = a*x + y` kernel on the
`cpu` device. Warp will not compile a kernel typed into `python -` (it
extracts the source with `inspect`, so "Directly evaluating Warp code
defined as a string using `exec()` is not supported"); it needs a file.

```
Warp 1.17.0 initialized:
   CUDA Toolkit 12.9, CUDA driver not available (NVRTC compilation available)
   Devices:
     "cpu"      : "x86_64"
warp 1.17.0 | devices: ['cpu'] | cuda available: False | init 0.02s
Module __main__ 4c00946 load on device 'cpu' took 1906.31 ms  (compiled)
first launch, including the JIT compile: 1.93s
10 more launches of a 10,000,000-element kernel: 26.8 ms each | y[0] = 22.0
real    0m2.643s
```

## Newton: the pendulum

The default example, the XPBD solver, no window (`--viewer null`), 200
frames, Newton's own `--benchmark` timer.

```bash
python -m newton.examples basic_pendulum --viewer null --device cpu --num-frames 200 --benchmark
```

Cold, with an empty kernel cache: **23.7 s** wall, almost all of it JIT
compilation — `newton._src.solvers.xpbd.kernels` 8.2 s,
`newton._src.sim.articulation` 4.2 s, the viewer kernels 2.4 s, the rest
under a second each — and then `Benchmark: 1454.3 FPS (197 frames in
0.14s)`. Warm, the same command a minute later: **2.95 s** wall, `1388.9
FPS`. The compiled modules live in `~/.cache/warp/1.17.0`.

The same scene written to OpenUSD instead of a window:

```bash
python -m newton.examples basic_pendulum --viewer usd --output-path pendulum.usd --device cpu --num-frames 200
```

3.3 s; `pendulum.usd`, 36,638 bytes, a binary crate file (`PXR-USDC`) —
the format Isaac Sim, Omniverse and Newton share.

## Newton: a quadruped from URDF

```bash
python -m newton.examples basic_urdf --viewer null --device cpu --num-frames 200 --benchmark
```

The example loads `quadruped.urdf` from Newton's bundled assets and uses
XPBD by default. **11.4 s** wall; the only new compile was the GJK/MPR
narrow phase (4.0 s); `Benchmark: 45.1 FPS (197 frames in 4.36s)`.

## Newton: an Allegro hand on MuJoCo Warp

```bash
python -m newton.examples robot_allegro_hand --viewer null --device cpu --num-frames 200 --benchmark
```

The example downloads the `wonik_allegro` asset (a left hand with a cube,
USDA), registers MuJoCo attributes and runs `SolverMuJoCo` — that is,
MuJoCo Warp, Newton's primary backend, on the CPU. **57.8 s** wall, of
which the MuJoCo Warp kernels' compilation was roughly 35 s (`mujoco_warp
._src.sensor` alone 2.9 s, dozens of small solver kernels at 0.1–0.4 s
each); then `Benchmark: 10.1 FPS (197 frames in 19.54s)`.

## The table

| Step | Wall time | Of which compile | Simulation |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pip install warp-lang "newton[examples]"` | 1 min 20 s | — | — |
| Warp, 10 M-element kernel | 2.6 s | 1.9 s | 26.8 ms per launch |
| Newton pendulum, XPBD, cold | 23.7 s | ≈ 20 s | 1,454 frames/s |
| Newton pendulum, XPBD, warm | 2.95 s | ≈ 0 | 1,389 frames/s |
| Newton pendulum → `pendulum.usd` | 3.3 s | ≈ 0 | 36 KB usdc |
| Newton quadruped (URDF), XPBD | 11.4 s | 4.0 s | 45 frames/s |
| Newton Allegro hand + cube, MuJoCo Warp | 57.8 s | ≈ 35 s | 10.1 frames/s |

A "frame" is one of the example's render steps; each holds several physics
substeps at the example's defaults, which were not changed.

## What this shows, and what it does not

- Everything the documentation says runs on a CPU did: Warp kernels, all
  three Newton solvers tried (XPBD, and MuJoCo Warp through `SolverMuJoCo`),
  URDF and USD import, USD export. No flag other than `--device cpu` and
  `--viewer null` was needed.
- The first run of anything is dominated by JIT compilation, which is
  cached; budget half a minute per new example, once.
- The numbers are for one copy of one robot on four cores. Newton's design
  point is thousands of copies on one GPU; 10 frames/s for a 16-joint hand
  is a reading speed, not a training speed. The CPU path is for reading the
  code, writing tests, and teaching — which is what the Robotics course on
  this site needs it for.
- Not run: anything needing Isaac Sim (no RTX GPU here, no macOS build
  anywhere), Isaac Lab's kit-less Newton mode (its 3.0 beta was not
  installed), GR00T or Cosmos inference (16–32 GB of VRAM).
